nameStory: Red clover gets its straightforward name from its rosy-pink to deep red flower heads that bloom throughout the growing season. The word 'clover' comes from the Old English 'clæfre,' referring to the plant's distinctive three-leaflet structure that has been recognized for centuries.
description: Red clover is a low-growing herbaceous plant that typically reaches 1-2 feet tall, forming loose patches in fields and along roadsides. Its most recognizable features are the globe-shaped pink to reddish-purple flower heads and the characteristic three-part leaves, each leaflet often marked with a pale chevron pattern. This non-native plant has become completely naturalized throughout New England, where it's a common sight in meadows, pastures, and disturbed areas. The plant has a somewhat sprawling growth habit with multiple stems arising from the base.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded flower heads about the size of a grape, colored deep pink to reddish-purple. The tiny individual flowers are tightly packed and feel soft and fuzzy to the touch, almost like a small pompom.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three oval leaflets per leaf, each typically marked with a distinctive pale green or whitish V-shaped chevron across the middle. The leaflets feel smooth and slightly waxy, and are broader than those of white clover.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright to semi-sprawling stems that can reach 1-2 feet tall, much taller than the creeping white clover. Multiple stems emerge from a central root system, creating loose clumps rather than tight mats.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hairy, somewhat thick stems that feel sturdy between your fingers. The stems are often tinged with red or purple, especially near the base and where leaves attach.

habitat: Red clover thrives in open, sunny locations throughout New England, especially in fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed soils. It prefers well-drained but moist soils and is commonly found from sea level to moderate elevations. You'll often see it mixed with grasses in hayfields, along woodland edges, and in areas that have been cleared or disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small three-leaflet clusters close to the ground. First flower heads begin appearing in late spring, starting as small green buds.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant rosy-pink flower heads throughout the summer months. This is the best time for identification when flowers are most vibrant and numerous.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, though less abundantly. Seed heads develop as brown, papery structures, and leaves may begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to ground level in most of New England, leaving only dried brown stems and seed heads that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Red clover flowers are actually tiny landing pads designed specifically for bumblebees - their long tongues are the perfect length to reach the nectar hidden deep inside each tiny flower, while honeybees' tongues are too short to reach it effectively!
confusionNotes: Red clover is most often confused with white clover, but red clover stands much taller (1-2 feet vs. staying low to the ground), has larger pink-red flower heads instead of white ones, and broader leaflets. Remember: red clover reaches your knee, white clover hugs your ankle.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'red' clover, the flowers are actually pink to reddish-purple, not true red. This European native has been in North America so long (brought by early colonists as livestock feed) that many people assume it's a native wildflower, but it's actually one of our most successful non-native plants.
compareHints: Among New England's clovers, red clover is the tallest and most upright, while white clover creeps along the ground and has white flowers. The various hop clovers have small yellow flowers in elongated clusters rather than the globe-shaped pink heads of red clover. Alsike clover is similar in size but has white flowers tinged with pink, and lacks the distinctive chevron markings on the leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England clovers, white clover is unique for its creeping growth habit and pure white spherical flowers.

Among New England clovers, rabbitfoot clover is unique for its fuzzy, pale, cylindrical flower heads - completely different from the round pink heads of red clover, the round white heads of white clover, or the small yellow clusters of hop clovers.
Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, large hop clover stands tallest and most erect, while hop trefoil sprawls closer to the ground with smaller flowers.

Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, hop trefoil stands out with its distinctive oval, hop-shaped flower heads compared to the round heads of large hop clover or the tiny heads of lesser hop trefoil.
Among New England's clovers, alsike is the tall one with color-changing flowers.
Among New England's clovers, lesser hop trefoil stands out for its tiny size and bright yellow flowers - most other clovers have white, pink, or red blooms.
Crimson clover stands out from other New England clovers by its distinctive torpedo-shaped, brilliant red flower heads - no other local clover has this intense crimson color or elongated cone shape.
Zigzag clover differs from red clover by having narrower leaflets without white markings and distinctive angled stems.
